newsitem.title: HONG KONG: PRESS DIGEST - H.K. newspaper editorials - Oct 3.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - H.K. newspaper editorials - Oct 3.

text.p: (NOTE: These are highlights of editorial comment carried in the Hong Kong press on Thursday. Views expressed are those of the newspapers quoted and do not represent an editorial viewpoint of Reuters).
With 271 days to go before the British colony reverts to China, the Hong Kong media focused mainly on the last policy address made by British Governor Chris Patten before the transition.

The middle of the road HONG KONG ECONOMIC TIMES said Patten's policy address was full of colour and talked about what other people had done and his anxiety towards the future, rather than his own work.
It said Patten's advise for his successor and the benchmarks by which he said the future government would be judged reflected accurately the concerns of Hong Kong people.
But, the paper said, the past was past and what the Governor had to do now was to ensure the handover went as smoothly and successfully as possible.

The HONG KONG ECONOMIC JOURNAL said Patten's report talked about the dedication of previous governors, but made no mention of the dirty deeds of the British government in the early days of colonial rule.
The paper also questioned whether Britain had really bequeathed other former colonies with good parliamentary systems, as the Governor said, or with endless trouble and infighting.
The SING TAO DAILY said that the report showed the anger, anxiety and frustration of the Governor, but these issues were not what Hong Kong people worried about.
The report, the paper said, scarely mentioned these worries which encompassed issues ranging from high property prices and the paucity of social welfare benefits.
It said as the handover approached, Hong Kong people wanted Beijing and London to talk rather than fight.

The Beijing-funded WEN WEI PO described Patten's address as "a colonialist eulogy of the last Governor". It said the report was actually a manifesto that praised Patten's political reforms and the more than 150 years of colonial rule, and was an effort to prolong British political influence in the territory.
The paper said it was impossible for Britain to maintain its political influence in Hong Kong and the British government should cooperate with China on handover issues.

The English-language SOUTH CHINA MORNING POST said the speech was reflective one, was uncompromising on democracy and freedom and was justifiably optimistic about the opportunities ahead. It said there was still plenty for Patten to do in the next nine months.
